proposals.relationship: Parr uses Bourdieu’s embodied history and habitus to explain how past practice persists in bodies and shapes later responses.
proposals.evidence_note: Own Sensing Changes 8–9 explicitly uses Bourdieu to move beyond bodies being conditioned by circumstances: they also hold past practice outside conscious memory and influence later action. Page 9 names habitus with Mauss’s prior work; 12 groups Bourdieu with Hayles, Maturana, Varela, Connerton, Lefebvre and Merleau-Ponty rather than giving him sole credit. This is a particular conceptual resource for the six case studies, not formal mentorship or a complete reading of Bourdieu. Preview ends after 23, so endnotes 14, 16, 24 and 41 are unavailable; visible markers are not claimed as read notes.
primary_locators: 2010 printed 8–9 and 12; actual printed 8/PDF leaf 38 visually checked; endnote markers only

proposals.relationship: Parr draws on Cronon’s warning about narrative’s rhetorical razor to make ecological and bodily knowledge a priority for environmental history.
proposals.evidence_note: Own 9–10 describes Cronon’s 1992 problem with linear narrative representing ecological nonlinearity and randomness, then explicitly agrees that these marginalized senses should be brought into environmental and technological history. Pages 13 and 20 reuse his caution and call to attend to autonomous nonhuman nature. This is Parr’s attributed reading and methodological use, not a claim that Cronon rejects all narrative or that she abandons language. She explicitly retains useful insights from literary scholarship on 8–9. Original Cronon works and absent endnotes 26/63 unread.
primary_locators: 2010 printed 9–10, 13 and 20; actual 20/PDF leaf 50 visually checked

proposals.relationship: Parr presents Corbin’s integrated histories of the sensing self as a model for recovering embodied knowledge of environments and technologies.
proposals.evidence_note: Own 11 calls Corbin the leading practitioner of sensory history and explains his shift from individual senses to the seaside and Pinagot’s natural and social landscapes, emphasizing synaesthesia. She makes that recovery specifically valuable to her project and continues on 12 with the complex specificity of bodies. This is an explicit methodological exemplar, not proof of direct contact or independent validation of every reconstruction. Actual Corbin books and absent endnotes 33–36 unread.
primary_locators: 2010 printed 11–12, paragraph beginning Because the senses and continuation complex specificity; endnote markers only

proposals.relationship: Parr uses Merchant’s contrasting accounts of Indigenous and Euro-American understandings of nature to develop her account of historically embodied environmental knowledge.
proposals.evidence_note: Own 19–20 gives Merchant’s interpretation of Native American forest gardening and regeneration alongside European Christian, scientific and capitalist conceptions of fallen nature. Parr uses this contrast to explain different bodily and epistemological relationships with environments before turning to Cronon and gender. These are Merchant’s broad historical interpretations as Parr employs them, not a newly certified uniform Indigenous worldview or a fresh reading of Merchant’s book. Original work and absent note 62 unread.
primary_locators: 2010 printed 19–20; first paragraph 20 completes the Merchant discussion

proposals.relationship: Parr uses Lefebvre’s reciprocal relation between material and social bodies to describe how corporeal and symbolic embodiment can work together.
proposals.evidence_note: Own 22 closes the introduction’s examples by saying the two modes often exist in tandem, then explicitly invokes Lefebvre’s reciprocal implication and explication. Page 23 makes recovering embodied histories the aim. The use qualifies a simple opposition between bodily knowledge and discourse; she does not discard social meaning. Lefebvre also appears in the jointly credited conceptual lineage on 12. This is a bounded conceptual resource, not a claim that his whole theory was adopted; original work and absent endnotes unread.
primary_locators: 2010 printed 12 and 22–23; actual 22/PDF leaf 52 visually checked

proposals.relationship: Parr challenges the discursive account of the body she attributes to Foucault and grounds her environmental histories in embodied knowledge that can elude textual representation.
proposals.evidence_note: Own 8 explicitly contrasts her assumptions with Foucault’s epistemological view of the body existing only in discourse. Pages 8–10 retain useful linguistic and literary insights while seeking material and sensory knowledge beyond them. This is Parr’s characterization and disagreement, not a finding that the complete Foucault corpus makes only that claim. The quoted formulation’s absent endnote 17 cannot be traced further from this preview, so no direct original quotation or source attribution beyond Parr is asserted.
primary_locators: 2010 printed 8–10, especially 8 paragraph beginning The next step; actual 8/PDF leaf 38 visually checked

proposals.relationship: Parr argues that the symbolic account of embodiment she attributes to Butler needs to be supplemented by the gendered bodily experience of work and environments.
proposals.evidence_note: Own 20 credits Butler’s insights in Gender Trouble and Bodies That Matter into power relations and the constraints gendered assumptions place on genetic research, then argues that gender is also made by active corporeal experience. Scott is explicitly credited alongside Butler; the criticism does not assert that all gender construction is false or that embodied differences are timeless biological essences. The title-specific discussion is Parr’s reading, with the complete originals and absent note 65 unread.
primary_locators: 2010 printed 20, paragraph beginning Scholarship on the social construction of gender; actual PDF leaf 50 visually checked; framing 8–12

proposals.relationship: Parr argues that Scott’s discursive account of gender should be supplemented by the bodily experience of historically different work and environments.
proposals.evidence_note: Own 20 links Scott’s gender-as-a-category argument to the epistemological premises of Butler’s work, then states that gender is also made through active experience and corporeal embodiment. Pages 8–12 explain this supplement while retaining useful linguistic insights and historically specific bodies. This is a bounded later disagreement with equal Butler credit, compatible with the earlier Scott resource already 1683; no wholesale reversal, naturalized sex roles or rejection of gender history is inferred. Scott’s original article and absent note 66 unread.
primary_locators: 2010 printed 20, Scott sentence and following But gender is also created; actual PDF leaf 50 visually checked; framing 8–12

proposals.relationship: Parr uses Carson’s Silent Spring as an example of conveying nature’s active response and humans’ reciprocal relationship with it.
proposals.evidence_note: Own 20 explicitly asks readers to consider how Carson’s depiction of active, responsive nature altered conceptions of biology, culture and environment. Parr uses this example within her argument for bodily environmental knowledge: a text can help urban readers recognize the reciprocity planters and gleaners knew through practice. This preserves the productive role of texts within her argument about embodiment; it does not claim personal contact, universal reception, or a fresh full reading of Silent Spring. The original book and absent notes 67–68 unread.
primary_locators: 2010 printed 20, paragraph beginning Consider how, in Silent Spring; actual PDF leaf 50 visually checked
